request.context: We have a Python microservice at `~/repos/order-gateway/src/external_clients/` that fans out requests to five third-party supplier APIs (inventory check, pricing, tax calculation, fraud scoring, and shipping estimation) before assembling a consolidated order quote. Right now if any one of those calls fails or hangs, the whole quote request blows up and the customer gets a 500. I need you to build a robust `resilient_client.py` module that wraps our existing `httpx.AsyncClient` calls with: (1) per-supplier configurable timeouts (connect vs. read vs. total), (2) a retry layer with exponential backoff plus jitter that respects each supplier's rate-limit headers (`Retry-After`, `X-RateLimit-Reset`), (3) a circuit breaker that trips open after N consecutive failures and periodically half-opens to probe recovery, and (4) a fallback strategy per supplier (e.g., return cached pricing, skip fraud scoring with a flag, use a default flat-rate shipping estimate). The retries should distinguish between transient errors (429, 502, 503, 504, `ConnectTimeout`, `ReadTimeout`) and permanent ones (400, 401, 404) that should fail immediately. Also include structured logging so we can trace every attempt, backoff delay, circuit state transition, and fallback activation per request-id. Write tests using `pytest` + `respx` that simulate flaky suppliers — random latency spikes, intermittent 503 bursts, rate-limit responses — and assert that the module converges to a successful quote within the configured budget of time and retries rather than cascading failures.

Make sure the style feels modern and matches what the Elixir community expects.

request.context: We have a background automation called "CodeSentinel" that monitors our GitHub repos for dependency vulnerabilities — when a new CVE is detected, it should automatically create a linear issue, post a Slack summary to #security-alerts, read the affected package's README from the repo, and generate a patch suggestion. Right now the whole thing runs as a hook that spawns a sub-agent via the SDK to do the heavy lifting, but I'm running into two problems: first, the hook's `onNotification` trigger is calling `claude` via the subprocess SDK pattern but it's not inheriting the right model configuration, so it defaults to the expensive model even for the triage step where haiku would suffice — how do I set the model and `maxTokens` properly in the SDK invocation from within a hook? Second, the sub-agent needs to chain together about six different tool calls (fetch GitHub file contents, search issues to avoid duplicates, create the issue, send the Slack message, read the project's security policy file, and write the patch file) and I keep getting tool-not-found errors for some of them. Can you give me the complete list of available tools that would cover this workflow — specifically which ones handle file reading from repos, issue/ticket creation, Slack messaging, file writing, and web fetching — and show me the correct hook code that spawns the background agent with cost-optimized model routing so the triage classification uses a cheap model but the patch generation step uses sonnet?

request.context: Search arXiv and PubMed for recent papers (2022-2024) on large language model applications in drug repurposing, and compile the key findings — specifically each paper's title, authors, year, method used, and reported accuracy metrics — into an Excel pivot table with calculated fields showing average accuracy by method type and year, plus slicers for filtering by publication venue and therapeutic area so our bioinfo team can use it as an interactive dashboard during next week's review meeting.
request.question: Which candidate skill is most relevant to satisfying this request?
answers: scientific - reviewer : comprehensive scientific document review and analysis. use when claude needs to review scientific papers, reports, preprints, or other research documents for : ( 1 ) identifying and evaluating claims and supporting evidence, ( 2 ) assessing logical argumentation and experimental design, ( 3 ) reviewing citation adequacy and suggesting additional references, ( 4 ) determining document type and research contribution, ( 5 ) checking technical accuracy and methodology, ( 6 ) providing constructive feedback on presentation and clarity. also handles language, grammar, and formatting review separately.

paper - to - code : implement ai / ml research papers from scratch when no official code exists. use when the user wants to reproduce a paper, implement an algorithm from a pdf, build a model architecture from a research paper, or create working code from academic publications. handles papers from arxiv, neurips, icml, iclr, cvpr, and other venues. produces uv - managed, gpu - ready python projects with tests, demos, and documentation.
academic - search : search academic paper repositories ( arxiv, semantic scholar ) for scholarly articles in physics, mathematics, computer science, quantitative biology, ai / ml, and related fields

materials - export : export materials data to professionally formatted excel files with auto - styling, filters, and priority column ordering. supports all search criteria from materials - search plus custom output options.
documentation - review : comprehensive checklist and process for reviewing documentation quality including voice, tone, structure, completeness, and technical accuracy.

smalltalk - implementation - finder : method implementation finder and analyzer for pharo smalltalk. provides expertise in discovering implementors across class hierarchies ( search _ implementors ), analyzing implementation patterns, learning coding idioms from existing implementations, assessing refactoring impact ( counting implementors and references ), finding duplicate code for consolidation, understanding abstract method implementations ( subclassresponsibility ), and tracing method overrides through inheritance chains. use when analyzing method implementations across classes, learning implementation idioms, assessing refactoring risk before changes, finding duplicate implementations for consolidation, understanding how abstract methods

odoo - model - inspector : this skill analyzes odoo model inheritance chains and fields, showing " who stands on whom " with complete inheritance hierarchy including all fields and methods from all modules. should be used when understanding model structure, checking available fields before adding new ones, or tracing inheritance dependencies.
bmad method : business model and architecture design methodology for aligning technical architecture with business model sustainability and scalability

github - issues : query and search github issues using gh cli with web fallback. supports filtering by labels, state, assignees, and full - text search. use when troubleshooting errors, checking if an issue is already reported, or finding workarounds.

arxiv - analysis : analyze arxiv research papers and explain them in accessible terms. use when the user mentions arxiv, research paper, academic paper, scientific paper, preprint, or provides an arxiv. org url.

model - evaluation : evaluates machine learning models for performance, fairness, and reliability using appropriate metrics and validation techniques. trigger keywords : model evaluation, metrics, accuracy, precision, recall, f1, roc, auc, cross - validation, ml testing.
review - skill - improver : analyzes feedback logs to identify patterns and suggest improvements to review skills. use when you have accumulated feedback data and want to improve review accuracy.

spec - verification : use during phase 5 of spec creation to verify completeness and accuracy before implementation - checks requirements accuracy, visual integration, reusability leverage, task specificity, and identifies over - engineering concerns

paper - search - usage : this skill should be used when user asks to " search for papers ", " find research papers ", " search arxiv ", " search pubmed ", " find academic papers ", " search ieee ", " search scopus ", or " look up scientific literature ".

request.context: Our real estate tech company is building a SwiftUI iPad app called "LeaseGuard" for commercial property managers to audit tenant lease compliance in the field. The app needs to track insurance certificate expirations (verifying CGL coverage minimums, additional insured endorsements), flag environmental compliance violations (hazmat storage, waste disposal covenants), monitor use clause adherence across retail tenants, and manage cure period deadlines with automated notice generation. I need help with two major pieces: First, architect the full navigation structure using NavigationSplitView with a three-column layout — sidebar lists properties, middle column shows tenant leases with compliance status badges, and detail column shows the specific audit findings. I need proper NavigationPath-based deep linking so that when a push notification fires about an expiring insurance certificate or a covenant breach cure period deadline, the app navigates directly to that tenant's compliance detail view. Include state restoration so auditors can pick up where they left off. Second, for the compliance engine layer, build out Swift models and logic for tracking all major lease obligation categories: insurance audits (CGL limits, umbrella requirements, workers comp, auto liability), environmental compliance checks against lease covenants, use clause violation detection (comparing permitted vs. actual use), and cure period countdown timers tied to notice requirements from the lease. The app also needs a Tab+Navigation structure using the iOS 18+ Tab API where the top-level tabs are Dashboard, Properties, Compliance Alerts, and Audit Reports — and I want to adopt Liquid Glass styling on iOS 26+ with graceful fallback for iOS 16-25. Show me the coordinator pattern for managing navigation state across tabs, the deep link handler, and the core compliance audit data models with example logic for flagging a tenant whose CGL policy dropped below the lease-required $2M per-occurrence limit.

request.context:
Our team maintains an open-source desktop app called AiderDesk at `~/repos/aiderdesk` (Electron + React + TypeScript, SCSS modules for styling). We need to do two things in a single PR and I'd like your help planning and implementing both. **First**, we want to add a new "Solarized Dark" UI theme — walk me through the full process from creating the SCSS file with CSS custom properties, updating the TypeScript theme type union, registering it in the theme factory/provider, and adding the i18n translation keys for the theme name and description in all our locale files (we support `en`, `de`, `ja`, `zh`). **Second**, before we open this PR we want to harden our entire Git workflow: we've had incidents with unsigned commits sneaking in, a `.env` file with Stripe keys almost making it to `main`, and a dependency confusion scare last quarter. Set up our repo with GPG/SSH commit signing enforcement (with a verification policy so CI rejects unsigned commits), configure a pre-commit and CI-level secret scanning pipeline (ideally catching secrets before they even hit the remote), add a branch protection ruleset that follows zero-trust principles (requiring reviews from CODEOWNERS, status checks, no force pushes, no bypasses even for admins), and recommend how we should handle tag signing for releases. I want all of this documented in a `SECURITY.md` and a contributor guide update so new contributors know exactly what's expected in 2025.
Please lay out a detailed, step-by-step implementation plan for both parts, and where possible, provide the actual code/config files I can drop into the repo. Specifically:

**For the Solarized Dark theme:**
- The actual SCSS file with the full set of CSS custom properties (base colors, surface/background, text, borders, accent, error/warning/success, scrollbar, shadow — following the Solarized Dark palette faithfully)
- The changes to our TypeScript `Theme` type union (currently in `src/types/theme.ts`) to include `'solarized-dark'`
- Registration in our theme provider so the new theme shows up in the settings dropdown, including the logic for applying/removing the CSS class on `<body>`
- All four locale files (`en.json`, `de.json`, `ja.json`, `zh.json`) with the new keys like `theme.solarizedDark.name` and `theme.solarizedDark.description`
- A brief Storybook story or manual test plan so we can visually verify the theme looks right

**For the Git security hardening:**
- A `.gitconfig` snippet (or setup script) that enforces GPG or SSH commit signing locally, with instructions for both GPG and SSH key-based signing (since some of our contributors prefer SSH keys for simplicity)
- A GitHub Actions workflow or CI check that verifies every commit in a PR is signed and rejects the PR if any aren't
- Pre-commit hooks (using something like `pre-commit` framework or husky + a custom script) that scan for secrets — covering patterns like AWS keys, Stripe keys, generic high-entropy strings, and `.env` file contents — so secrets get caught *before* a push
- A recommended `.gitignore` update to make sure `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.*.local`, and any key/cert files are excluded
- A GitHub branch protection ruleset (as JSON or step-by-step UI instructions) for `main` and `release/*` that enforces: required signed commits, at least 2 approving reviews from CODEOWNERS, all status checks passing, no force pushes, no deletions, no bypass list (even for org admins), and dismiss stale reviews on new pushes

request.context: Our multi-tenant SaaS analytics platform on GKE (`~/infra/k8s/`) needs a comprehensive autoscaling setup and I'm struggling to get all the pieces working together. We have three tiers of workloads: (1) a stateless API gateway deployment that should scale based on requests-per-second from a Prometheus custom metric (`http_requests_per_second`), targeting 500 rps per pod, scaling between 3–40 replicas; (2) a set of GPU-equipped ML inference node pools that should scale the underlying GKE node pool up/down based on a pending-pods signal but also have a scheduled scale-up every weekday at 8am EST to pre-warm 4 GPU nodes before the morning traffic spike, scaling back down to 1 node at 10pm; and (3) Cloud Run services handling async report generation that should scale to zero when idle but burst up to 100 instances, with a concurrency of 1 per instance and a custom scaling metric based on our Pub/Sub subscription backlog depth. Can you write out the full manifests and configs — HPAs with custom metrics adapters, cluster autoscaler profiles, the CronJob or scheduled scaling policies for the GPU pool, and the Cloud Run service YAML with the Pub/Sub trigger — and explain how these three layers interact so we don't get into a situation where the cluster autoscaler and the HPA fight each other?

The goal is to migrate everything from NumPy 1.x to NumPy 2.0 (handling all the deprecated API removals and namespace changes), simultaneously replace our homegrown logging with structlog across all packages, and upgrade our test suite from unittest-style to pytest with fixtures. These three workstreams touch almost every file but are largely independent of each other. I'd like you to set up a plan where each workstream runs as its own branch with a dedicated session, define the merge order so we don't get hellish conflicts (since some files will be touched by more than one workstream — especially the `__init__.py` files and the CI config), and create a validation gate after each merge step that runs the full test suite plus type checking before the next branch comes in. For the NumPy migration branch, pay special attention to `atlas-linalg` since it uses `numpy.distutils` which is completely removed. For the structlog branch, we need a shared logging config module in a new `atlas-common` package that all six packages depend on. And for the pytest migration, convert the custom test runners in `ci/run_tests.sh` as well. Can you lay out the full coordination plan, create the initial branch structure, and then kick off all three workstreams?

Our QA team needs a nightly job that scrapes pricing data from three competitor e-commerce sites (all heavily protected with Cloudflare and DataDome anti-bot measures), captures full-page screenshots of each product listing page for audit trails, and then cross-references the scraped prices against our own catalog via our internal pricing MCP server and inventory MCP server to flag any items where we're more than 15% higher — finally it should file tickets automatically through our Jira MCP server for each flagged item. The competitors use infinite-scroll product pages and one of them requires logging in to see wholesale pricing tiers. Can you build this as a single TypeScript script I can run locally on my Ubuntu 24.04 workstation? Last time I tried Playwright on this machine I kept getting "target closed" errors and the headless browser would hang indefinitely on the infinite scroll pages, so please make sure those issues are handled. Also the Cloudflare-protected sites were detecting the automation immediately — I need stealth mode or whatever fingerprint evasion actually works with Playwright v1.57.
I also need the script to handle the login flow for the wholesale site (WholesaleDirect — they have a standard email/password form with a CAPTCHA that only triggers on suspicious sessions, so hopefully stealth mode avoids that). 

Here's more specifics on what I need:

1. **Anti-detection**: I've heard `playwright-extra` with the stealth plugin is outdated. What's the current best approach for Playwright 1.57 to avoid Cloudflare and DataDome detection? I need realistic browser fingerprints, proper TLS fingerprinting, and human-like mouse movements and scroll behavior. If I need to use a specific launch configuration or browser channel (like `chrome` instead of `chromium`), tell me exactly what to set.

2. **Infinite scroll handling**: The three sites are:
   - `competitorA.com/products` — lazy loads 20 items at a time on scroll
   - `competitorB.com/catalog` — uses intersection observer, loads 50 items per batch
   - `wholesaledirect.com/pricing` (requires login) — virtual scroll with ~2000 items total
   
   I need robust scroll logic that doesn't hang. Set a maximum wait timeout per scroll increment (like 5 seconds), detect when no new items are loading, and bail out after 60 seconds total per page. The "target closed" errors I was getting before seemed related to the page crashing during long scroll operations — maybe memory related?

3. **Screenshots**: Full-page screenshots saved as PNGs with timestamps in the filename, stored in `./audit_screenshots/YYYY-MM-DD/`.

4. **Price cross-referencing**: After scraping, I need to call our internal pricing service to get our current prices for matching SKUs, and also check inventory levels so we don't flag out-of-stock items. Both of these are exposed as MCP servers on our internal network — the pricing one is at `http://pricing.internal:3100/mcp` and the inventory one is at `http://inventory.internal:3200/mcp`. The pricing server has a `get_prices_by_sku` tool and the inventory server has a `check_stock_levels` tool.

request.context: We're building a customer support chatbot at `~/repos/support-bot` using Python/LangChain. Right now our retrieval pipeline pulls chunks from our Zendesk knowledge base stored in Pinecone, but the answers are often wrong or hallucinated — the LLM ignores retrieved context or cites the wrong article. Can you refactor our `retrieval_chain.py` to implement a more robust RAG pipeline? Specifically: (1) switch from naive top-k similarity search to hybrid search combining dense embeddings with BM25 keyword matching, (2) add a re-ranking step using a cross-encoder before passing context to the LLM, (3) restructure the prompt template so the model is explicitly grounded on the retrieved documents and refuses to answer if no relevant context is found, (4) include inline citations in the response that link back to the specific Zendesk article ID and section each claim comes from, and (5) add a simple faithfulness check that verifies each generated sentence is actually supported by the retrieved chunks before returning the response to the user. Our current stack is LangChain 0.2, OpenAI embeddings, Pinecone vector store, and GPT-4o.

request.context: We have a Neo4j knowledge graph at `~/repos/company-kg` that was populated from three different data sources — our CRM (Salesforce exports), our procurement system (SAP CSVs), and a manually curated spreadsheet from the partnerships team. The problem is that the same real-world companies, people, and locations appear as separate nodes with slightly different names, spellings, or metadata across these sources (e.g., "IBM Corp", "International Business Machines", "IBM Corporation" are three distinct nodes, or "J. Smith" and "John Smith" from the same org). Can you write a Python script using `py2neo` that detects and merges these duplicate entities? I'd like it to use fuzzy string matching on names, plus heuristic rules based on shared attributes like address, domain, tax ID, or linked relationships to determine confidence scores for potential merges. It should output a ranked list of candidate pairs above a configurable threshold, and then have a `--apply` flag that actually executes the merges in Neo4j by consolidating properties and re-linking all relationships to the surviving canonical node. Make sure it logs every merge action for auditability.

request.context:
Hey, I'm working on an ESP32-based weather station project using Arduino IDE and I just fixed a bug in our `sensor_calibration.cpp` where the BMP280 readings were off by a constant offset — I adjusted the compensation formula and updated the altitude calculation. I tried to compile before committing but I'm getting this wall of errors I can't parse. Here's what the compiler spits out:
```
src/sensor_calibration.cpp: In function 'float getCompensatedPressure(int32_t)':
src/sensor_calibration.cpp:47:23: error: 'dig_P9' was not declared in this scope
   float pressure = (adc_P / 16384.0 - dig_T1 / 1024.0) * dig_P9;
                       ^~~~~~
src/sensor_calibration.cpp:52:9: error: expected ';' before 'float'
   float altitude = 44330.0 * (1.0 - pow(pressure / SEA_LEVEL_HPA, 0.1903))
         ^~~~~
src/sensor_calibration.cpp:58:1: error: expected '}' at end of input
 }
 ^
src/sensor_calibration.cpp:34:12: warning: unused variable 'temp_offset' [-Wunused-variable]
   float temp_offset = calibration_data.offset;
            ^~~~~~~~~~~
```

I honestly can't tell what's going wrong here — especially that "expected '}' at end of input" one because when I look at the code all my braces seem matched. Can you help me understand what each of these errors actually means and what I likely messed up?

Also, once I get this sorted and it compiles clean, I want to commit the changes with a good message. The gist of what I did is:
- Fixed BMP280 pressure compensation formula that was producing readings ~3 hPa too high
- Updated altitude calculation to use the corrected pressure values
- Moved calibration coefficients into the `BMP280CalibrationData` struct instead of using loose globals

Can you help me craft and make the commit for these changes?

request.context: We have a Next.js 14 app (App Router) for our restaurant chain's online ordering platform that we need to deploy to Vercel. The app uses Edge Functions for geolocation-based menu pricing, serverless API routes that connect to a Neon Postgres database via Prisma, and we need a cron job that runs nightly at 2 AM UTC to sync our menu catalog from a third-party POS system. We also have environment variables for Stripe, our POS API keys, and database connection strings that differ between preview and production. Can you walk me through the full deployment setup — including the `vercel.json` configuration, how to structure the edge and serverless functions so they don't hit size/timeout limits, the cron job definition, proper env var configuration across environments, and any production optimizations like ISR revalidation or middleware for regional routing? We've been running this locally and on a VPS but want to move everything to Vercel properly.

request.context: Our team is building an ML-powered image classification API at `~/repos/vision-api` using Hono on Cloudflare Workers. I need two things done: First, set up the Hono server with a proper middleware chain — we need a custom auth middleware that validates JWT tokens and attaches user info to the context, a rate-limiting middleware (100 requests/min per API key), CORS configured for our frontend origins, and a request logging middleware. Make sure the execution order is correct so auth runs before rate limiting. The main `POST /classify` endpoint should accept an image upload, validate it in middleware, then queue an inference job. Second, the actual model inference is too heavy for Workers — I need to run our PyTorch ResNet50 fine-tuned model on a cloud GPU. Set up a `gpu.toml` config targeting a RunPod A100 instance, write the inference worker script (`inference/run.py`) that loads the model checkpoint from S3 and serves predictions via a simple HTTP endpoint, and give me the GPU CLI commands to deploy it, check pod status, and stream logs. The Hono endpoint should call out to the RunPod inference pod's URL. Show me the full project structure and how these two pieces connect.

request.context:
Can you pull together a competitive landscape analysis for the North American cold-pressed juice market? I need estimated market size (2020–2024), CAGR projections through 2030, the top 10 brands by revenue share, and a breakdown of distribution channels (DTC, grocery, foodservice). Also identify any whitespace opportunities in functional/adaptogenic juice blends — I want to know if there's an underserved price tier or demographic segment we could target for a new product line launching Q2 2026.
Additionally, if you can flag any emerging trends around sugar reduction, sustainability packaging, or HPP (high-pressure processing) adoption rates among competitors, that would be really valuable for our positioning strategy. 

For the demographic analysis, I'm especially interested in Gen Z and millennial purchasing behavior — average basket size, purchase frequency, and willingness to pay premium pricing ($8-12 per bottle range) for functional benefits like stress relief, gut health, or immunity support.

If there's relevant data on how brands like Suja, Pressed Juicery, or Evolution Fresh have shifted their product mix over the last 2-3 years, include that too. We're trying to figure out whether to enter at a premium tier with adaptogens (ashwagandha, reishi, lion's mane blends) or go mid-market with a simpler functional positioning.

Finally, can you summarize everything in a format I can drop into a pitch deck — key stats, a competitor matrix, and 3-5 bullet points on the whitespace opportunity?

request.context: We're deploying our SaaS billing microservice at `~/repos/subscription-engine` to a Kubernetes cluster and need two things wired up. First, the service handles recurring subscriptions through Stripe (credit cards, SCA/3DS flows), PayPal billing agreements, and we're adding LemonSqueezy as a third provider for international customers. Each provider has its own webhook endpoint for payment events (invoice.paid, subscription.canceled, disputes, etc.) and we need a unified webhook ingestion layer that validates signatures, normalizes events into a common schema, and routes them to our event bus — making sure we're not logging or persisting raw card numbers anywhere to stay PCI-compliant. Second, we need proper Kubernetes health check endpoints: a `/healthz` liveness probe that confirms the process isn't deadlocked, a `/readyz` readiness probe that verifies active connections to Postgres, Redis, and all three payment provider APIs (so we don't receive traffic if Stripe's SDK can't authenticate, for example), and a `/startupz` startup probe with a higher failure threshold since the initial webhook signature key fetch from each provider takes 15-20 seconds on cold boot. Can you set up the Express routes for all of this, the Helm chart probe configuration with appropriate timeouts/thresholds, and the webhook handler architecture with idempotency keys to prevent duplicate charge processing?

I've been considering a few approaches: (1) switching to CSS Modules with aggressive code-splitting, (2) using Critters or a similar tool to inline critical CSS and defer the rest, (3) refactoring our Tailwind config to purge more aggressively and reduce custom utility layers, or (4) moving to vanilla-extract with zero-runtime CSS generation. Can you review the tradeoffs of each approach for our situation — factoring in selector complexity, unused CSS elimination, bundle size impact, and render-blocking behavior — and recommend a concrete migration plan with the specific config changes and architectural restructuring we'd need across our layout files, global styles, and component library?

request.context: Hey, can you review the terrain rendering shader in our open-world game project at `~/repos/horizon-craft/src/shaders/terrain.glsl`? It's a single 400-line file that handles vertex displacement from a heightmap, triplanar texture blending, fog, water edge blending, dynamic day-night lighting, and shadow mapping — all crammed into one vertex and one fragment shader with about 30 uniforms. The original dev left and nobody wants to touch it because changing the fog always breaks the water edge effect and vice versa. I suspect there are duplicated transformation calculations between the vertex and fragment stages, some varyings that are computed but never actually read, and a bunch of magic numbers for things like fog density and blend falloff that are hardcoded instead of passed as uniforms. There also seem to be multiple `vec4` uniforms that could be grouped into a struct or UBO. request.context: We're about to ship a set of custom Webflow Code Components (a React-based card carousel and an interactive pricing calculator) via `webflow library share`, but before we do, I need two things handled in one pass. First, run a full pre-deployment validation on both components — check the bundle sizes are under Webflow's limits, verify all prop configurations and slot definitions are correct, confirm there are no SSR-incompatible hooks or browser-only APIs in the initial render path, make sure our Tailwind styles aren't leaking globally, and flag any dependency issues (we're importing `framer-motion` and `recharts` so I want to know if those bloat the bundle or break in Webflow's runtime). Second, we deploy these components through an Ansible playbook that provisions a staging Webflow workspace and pushes environment-specific API keys (Stripe publishable keys, analytics IDs, and a CMS read token) into the component config. Right now the keys are hardcoded in `group_vars/all.yml` as plain text, which is terrible. I need you to refactor the playbook to pull all secrets from our Infisical vault using a reusable lookup task pattern, add `no_log: true` on every task that handles credentials, and set up a fallback chain so if Infisical is unreachable it tries the local encrypted vault file before failing. Show me the complete validated component checklist plus the refactored playbook with the secrets integration.

request.context: We're designing "PromptForge," an internal platform where our product teams can compose, version, and A/B-test prompts that get sent to various LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral). Right now we have a rough requirements doc but no architecture yet. I need two things from you: First, walk me through the key prompt engineering principles we should bake directly into the platform's UX — things like structured instruction formatting, role-setting, chain-of-thought scaffolding, anti-patterns to warn users about, and quality checklist gates that block a prompt from being promoted to production if it doesn't meet a minimum bar. We want the platform itself to guide users toward writing better prompts rather than relying on tribal knowledge. Second, based on those principles and the fact that we expect ~200 concurrent users, prompts versioned in Git, evaluation pipelines running nightly, and integration with our existing FastAPI + PostgreSQL + Redis stack, propose 2-3 architecture approaches for the backend (monolith vs. microservices vs. event-driven, how prompt templates and evaluation results are stored, caching strategy for LLM responses, how we handle multi-provider routing). Lay out the trade-offs for each approach — latency, operational complexity, cost, extensibility — so I can make a call on which direction to go before the team starts coding.

request.context: Our deployment pipeline for a Kubernetes-based log aggregation service keeps failing intermittently. Here's what's happening: we use AWS MCP tools to provision and manage EKS clusters and S3 buckets for log storage, but roughly every 8 hours the Terraform apply and aws-cli commands start throwing `UnauthorizedSSOTokenError` / `Token has expired` errors and the whole CI/CD run dies — we need the pipeline to detect that and automatically re-authenticate so overnight deploys don't just silently fail. Second, we want to stand up a proper error tracking and observability stack around this service: structured JSON logging from our Go microservices into OpenSearch, Sentry for exception capture with custom fingerprinting rules so we can group errors by tenant ID, and PagerDuty alerting thresholds (e.g., if any single tenant's error rate exceeds 5% over a 10-minute window). I need help writing the Sentry SDK integration code, the OpenSearch index template with appropriate field mappings for trace IDs and tenant context, and the alert routing rules. Third — and this is the urgent one — several of our engineers who use Ghostty as their terminal are reporting that it crashes with a segfault whenever they run `kubectl logs -f` against pods in this service that emit high-throughput structured logs (thousands of lines per second with ANSI color codes). I've got a core dump and the crash log showing it dies in the font shaping path, seemingly triggered by a specific UTF-8 sequence our JSON logger emits. Can you help me analyze the crash dump to find the root cause, suggest a workaround (maybe a Ghostty config tweak or filtering the output), and also file a useful bug report? I'd like all three of these tackled together since they're blocking our team's ability to ship the v2.3 release of the log platform this sprint.

request.context: Our nonprofit NABIP (National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals) is building an AMS on Supabase, and we're tackling three things at once. First, we need a new Supabase migration that adds tables for tracking CE (Continuing Education) course completions linked to members and chapters — each completion should reference the member, the course, the chapter that hosted it, and include a credit_hours numeric field and a completed_at timestamp. We need RLS policies so chapter admins can only see completions for their own chapter's members, and national admins see everything. Please validate that the schema fits with our existing member/chapter hierarchy and financial models. Second, we're writing BDD acceptance criteria in Gherkin (we use Reqnroll in our .NET test suite) for the feature where a chapter admin marks a member's course as completed and the system awards CE credits. I need scenarios covering the happy path, a case where the member already has that course completed (duplicate prevention), and a case where a non-admin tries to mark completion and gets denied. Third, we're building an MCP server that exposes our CE completion data as resources so that partner organizations can query a member's transcript. I need you to design the MCP tool and resource definitions — the server should expose a `ce-transcript` resource parameterized by member ID and a `record-completion` tool that chapter admins can invoke. Make sure the implementation follows the latest MCP spec for JSON-RPC 2.0 compliance, uses proper capability negotiation, and has appropriate auth/security patterns for the transport layer. Can you give me all three pieces together so they're consistent with each other?

request.context: Our insurance claims platform at `~/repos/claims-core` needs a major architectural change. Right now we have a traditional CRUD-based PostgreSQL setup for managing insurance claims, but auditors and regulators keep asking us for full claim lifecycle histories — every status change, every adjuster reassignment, every payout adjustment, with exact timestamps — and our current `updated_at` columns just aren't cutting it. We also need to support "as-of" queries like "show me the state of claim #4821 as it existed on March 3rd at 2pm" for dispute resolution. I want you to redesign the claims domain using an append-only event store (we'll stick with PostgreSQL using a `claim_events` table with `aggregate_id`, `aggregate_version`, `event_type`, `payload`, `occurred_at`), define the `ClaimAggregate` that reconstitutes state by replaying events (`ClaimFiled`, `ClaimAssigned`, `DocumentAttached`, `PayoutApproved`, `PayoutAdjusted`, `ClaimDenied`, `ClaimClosed`, `ClaimReopened`), enforce invariants in the aggregate (e.g., can't approve payout on a closed claim, can't reopen a denied claim older than 90 days), and build read-side projections into denormalized tables for the dashboard (`active_claims_view`, `adjuster_workload_view`, `monthly_payout_summary`). The projection rebuilder should be idempotent so we can replay from scratch if a projection schema changes. Use Python with SQLAlchemy for the write side and read projections, and include a small FastAPI layer with separate command endpoints (write) and query endpoints (read) to keep the CQRS separation clean. Also add a `TemporalQueryService` that can reconstruct any claim's state at an arbitrary point in time by replaying events up to that timestamp. Please include tests that verify aggregate invariants, event ordering, and that projections stay consistent after replaying the full event stream.

request.context: Our Python/FastAPI service "FleetPulse" tracks GPS positions for ~40,000 delivery vehicles and serves real-time ETAs. We're seeing P99 response times spike to 3+ seconds during peak hours. The main bottleneck is the `get_vehicle_eta` endpoint, which on every request queries PostGIS for the vehicle's current position, calls the Google Directions API for route calculation, and then does a weather lookup via OpenWeatherMap — none of this is cached. We also recompute a "traffic zone heatmap" (aggregated from all active vehicles) on every dashboard load, which hammers Postgres. I'd like you to design and implement a multi-layer caching strategy for this service. Specifically: (1) Add Redis-based caching for individual vehicle positions with an appropriate TTL given that GPS pings arrive every 15 seconds, (2) cache Google Directions responses with a key scheme that accounts for origin/destination snapping to a grid so nearby requests get cache hits, (3) implement a precomputed traffic heatmap that refreshes on a background schedule instead of per-request, (4) add cache invalidation logic so that when a vehicle reports a significant route deviation the stale ETA is evicted immediately, and (5) set up Prometheus metrics to track hit/miss ratios, cache size, and latency improvements. Show me the full implementation with the Redis integration, the background refresh worker, the invalidation signals, and the monitoring setup.

request.context: Our ed-tech startup is building a CLI tool with OpenAI Codex that lets curriculum designers generate and validate quiz content programmatically. Right now I'm architecting the `assess-gen` module and want to think through the design before coding. The core challenge: we serve learners in 14 languages (including RTL languages like Arabic and Urdu), and our quizzes need to be culturally and linguistically fair — a math word problem about "baseball statistics" obviously doesn't translate well to a Bengali-speaking student in Dhaka. I need help evaluating my current plan: (1) a JSON schema for assessment items that includes locale metadata, cultural-context tags, and difficulty anchors independent of language, (2) a validation pipeline that flags items with language-dependent idioms, culturally specific references, or constructs that change difficulty when translated (like questions relying on English homophones), and (3) an equivalence-check step that uses back-translation plus statistical item analysis to confirm that translated versions measure the same construct at the same difficulty level. Can you poke holes in this architecture, suggest what I'm missing for true cross-lingual fairness, and then help me scaffold the Python CLI tool structure — entry points, config, the validation engine, and the equivalence checker — so I can start implementing with Codex as my pair programmer?

request.context: Our data science team has a Python-based document processing pipeline at `~/repos/doc-intelligence` that we need to deploy to the edge. The pipeline has three stages: (1) a lightweight OCR preprocessing step, (2) a GPU-accelerated ML model that classifies and extracts entities from scanned PDFs, and (3) a summarization step using a fine-tuned LLM. We want the OCR step running as a Python Worker on Cloudflare for low-latency intake from global users, the ML classification running in a Cloudflare GPU container, and the summarization in a separate container. Each stage needs to pass results to the next via service bindings, and the whole thing should be wrapped in a durable workflow so that if the GPU container cold-starts or times out, the pipeline retries from where it left off instead of reprocessing from scratch. We also need an orchestrator that can run multiple documents through this pipeline in parallel (up to 20 concurrent), with a dashboard or status endpoint showing which documents are at which stage, which ones failed, and allowing us to pause/resume the entire batch. Can you set up the full architecture — wrangler configs, Dockerfiles for both containers, the Python Worker code with Pyodide, the workflow definition with retry logic, the service bindings between all components, environment variable management for API keys across stages, and the orchestration layer that coordinates the parallel document flows with visibility into their state?

request.context: We're building a digital archive for a retired investigative journalist's 30-year career at `~/repos/martinez-archive/`. The collection includes ~4,000 articles, interview transcripts, and source documents across topics like immigration policy, labor rights, and local government corruption. Second, the archive will have a public-facing companion YouTube channel where we release short video essays about key investigative stories from the collection. For the first three videos, I need eye-catching thumbnails designed: one about a 2003 meatpacking plant exposé, one about a series on municipal corruption in Phoenix from 2010-2014, and one about immigrant worker exploitation at agricultural operations. Each thumbnail should be optimized for click-through rate with strong contrast, readable text overlays, and a documentary/serious journalism aesthetic rather than clickbait. We also call an external geocoding API to enrich each reading with location data but have zero rate limiting on outbound calls, meaning a burst of incoming payloads can blow through our API quota in minutes and rack up massive overage charges. Can you review these patterns, explain the specific resource exhaustion and denial-of-service risks each one poses (memory, CPU, network, API cost), and then rewrite the relevant FastAPI endpoint code with proper safeguards — request body size limits, pagination for batch replay, connection caps and timeouts on SSE, and an async rate limiter for the outbound geocoding calls? Use Python 3.11 idioms and include tests that verify each protection actually rejects or throttles abusive input.

request.context: We're preparing to deploy v2.4.0 of our "FitPulse" fitness platform (Django/DRF backend, PostgreSQL, Redis, Celery workers) this Friday. Before we go live, I need two things done simultaneously. First, run through our full pre-deployment security checklist: verify that CSRF protection is correctly enforced on all state-changing endpoints, test the rate limiting on our `/api/auth/login` and `/api/auth/register` routes (we're targeting max 5 requests/minute per IP), validate input sanitization on the workout log submission forms (especially the free-text "notes" field), check that all security headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Strict-Transport-Security) are present and correctly configured, and audit our session management for proper cookie flags. Second, our platform has a background Celery job that runs nightly to compute weekly training load aggregates per user — the system is supposed to flag any user whose cumulative training volume (sets × reps × weight) spikes more than 20-30% week-over-week and emit a safety warning to both the user's dashboard and our internal monitoring Slack channel. I need you to review the current implementation of that anomaly detection logic, write tests that simulate realistic weekly load data including edge cases (exactly 20% increase, 30% increase, gradual ramp-ups that cross the threshold mid-week, and sudden spikes from deload weeks), verify the safety flag emissions are correctly formatted and routed, and confirm that the conservative adjustment recommendations we surface to users are sensible (e.g., suggesting a 10% volume reduction rather than maintaining the spike). Can you handle both the security verification pass and the load anomaly guard validation together so we have a unified pre-deployment report?

request.context: Our e-commerce storefront "ThreadVine" is built with Tailwind CSS and the production CSS bundle has ballooned to over 380KB — page load times are suffering especially on mobile. We're currently on Tailwind v3 using `@apply` heavily inside component stylesheets, have a lot of unused utility classes leaking through from our shared UI library, and our `tailwind.config.js` has grown to include dozens of custom theme extensions and plugins. I want to migrate to Tailwind v4 and simultaneously optimize the entire CSS delivery pipeline. Can you walk me through a concrete plan covering: how to leverage v4's new engine and automatic content detection to eliminate the manual `content` config, replacing our excessive `@apply` usage with a more performant pattern, setting up proper tree-shaking so the shared UI library only contributes the classes actually used by ThreadVine, configuring CSS layers and cascade priorities correctly for v4, and any build-level optimizations (like splitting critical above-the-fold CSS from the rest) to get that bundle under 50KB for initial paint? Code examples for the migration steps and the final build config would be great.

Second, set up dev environment configs — we need a `.node-version` file pinned to Node 20 LTS, a `mise.toml` (some folks use mise, others asdf) with Node + pnpm versions, an `.env.template` with all required vars documented (DATABASE_URL, STRIPE_KEY, NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL, etc.), a bootstrap `scripts/setup.sh` that installs dependencies and runs DB migrations, and a `CONTRIBUTING.md` with onboarding steps for new devs. Third, write comprehensive tests for our `BreweryService` domain logic — specifically the `calculateTapRotation()` method that determines which beers to swap based on sales velocity, keg levels, and seasonal preferences, and the `processTabSettlement()` method that handles splitting tabs with tax and tip calculations. Use Given-When-Then structure, cover edge cases like empty kegs mid-rotation and partial tab payments, and set up the test files following our existing Jest + Testing Library patterns. Can you tackle all three of these together?

request.context: Design an autonomous iOS agent in Swift that monitors our app "TypeCraft" (a typography education tool) and automatically adjusts all text elements to comply with Apple's Human Interface Guidelines for iOS 26 — specifically San Francisco font usage, Dynamic Type scaling, proper tracking/leading values per text style (Large Title, Body, Caption, etc.), and correct optical sizing. The agent should run a continuous ReAct-style loop: observe the current screen hierarchy, reason about which labels/text views deviate from the HIG spec (wrong point size for a given text style, incorrect tracking at a specific optical size, missing Dynamic Type support, improper leading for a locale like Arabic or Thai), plan corrective actions, apply fixes via our internal styling API, then verify the changes actually rendered correctly by re-inspecting the view hierarchy. It needs goal decomposition so it can break "make all typography HIG-compliant" into subtasks per screen, a reflection/self-correction mechanism so that if a fix causes truncation or accessibility regressions it rolls back and tries an alternative approach, and a reliability strategy to handle the compounding error problem — if it's checking 40+ screens with dozens of text elements each, one bad decision shouldn't cascade. Include exponential backoff on failed corrections, confidence thresholds for when to apply changes autonomously vs. flag for human review, and structured logging of every observe-think-act cycle. Make sure the tracking table matches the iOS 26 San Francisco specifications exactly (e.g., Body at 17pt with 0.0 tracking, Caption2 at 11pt with +0.07 tracking, etc.) and that the agent handles SF Pro, SF Pro Rounded, SF Mono, and SF Compact variants correctly.

Everything should be PR-ready with proper CI checks.

request.context: We have a Julia package called `SpectrumTag` that generates deterministic color labels for RF spectrum allocation IDs. Right now we're using `Random.MersenneTwister` seeded with a hash of the allocation ID, but we want to switch to Gay.jl so each ID gets a reproducible color fingerprint. The idea is: take a 48-bit allocation ID, feed it into a SplitMix64-seeded Gay color generator, produce a GF(3) trit sequence that encodes the color as an SPI-compliant fingerprint, and then output both the hex color string and the raw trit vector. Can you write a module that does this? Specifically I need: (1) a function `color_fingerprint(alloc_id::UInt64)` that initializes the SplitMix64 RNG from Gay.jl with the allocation ID as seed, generates the deterministic color, converts the RGB channels into a balanced ternary (GF(3)) trit representation, and returns a named tuple with the hex color and a `Vector{Int8}` of trits; (2) a function `verify_spi_compliance(trits::Vector{Int8})` that checks the trit sequence against the SPI fingerprint constraints (valid trit values, correct length, checksum); and (3) a batch function that processes a `DataFrame` of allocation IDs and appends columns for the color and fingerprint. I also want tests that confirm two calls with the same ID always produce identical output and that different IDs produce distinct fingerprints with high probability.
